title: Find the Investor Who Can Actually Lead Your Seed Round
summary: Find the Investor Who Can Actually Lead Your Seed Round
body_markdown:
A founder can have ten good investor meetings and still be at zero. The meetings are real. The compliments are real. The missing thing is a decision somebody else can act on. If everyone says they would be interested once a round comes together, you have a group of people waiting for the same event.


## Work backward from the first close


Suppose you want to raise $2 million. You can start by asking how many investors you need. A better question is what would make this round real enough for the next person to decide. A $900,000 commitment from someone who will do the work to close is different from nine people saying they might put in $100,000. The sum on your spreadsheet can be the same while the state of the round is completely different.


Write down the minimum first close that changes what your company can do. It should buy a specific experiment or operating milestone, with room for it to take longer than you expect. Then work backward to the size and kind of commitment you need. This keeps you from chasing a recognizable name whose normal check cannot solve the problem.


## Read a deal, not just a thesis


A firm’s stage page helps you avoid obvious mismatches. A financing announcement often tells you more. Find a company close enough to yours to make the comparison useful. Was the firm named as lead, co-lead, or participant? Who from the firm was involved? Was this its first investment in the company? A follow-on in a company the firm already knows says little about what it will do for a founder it has never met.


Some firms describe the difference clearly.[Uncork](https://uncorkcapital.com/approach) says it often leads seed rounds and posts an initial check range.[Pear](https://pear.vc/how-we-invest/) describes both lead and co-lead investing.[focal](https://focal.vc/frequently-asked-questions/) presents itself as a first lead at inception. Those are three starting points, not three promises. Match the particular partner, current fund and plausible check to your own round before asking for a meeting.


## Ask a question that can change your plan


Try: ‘If this is a fit, what would your firm need before making the first material commitment?’ You want to learn who decides, what evidence is missing and whether the decision can happen while the round is open. If the answer is ‘come back with a lead,’ thank them, move them to the follower column and keep going. You still learned something useful.


Put three facts next to each name: evidence they can lead, why this deal fits, and the next thing you can do. Ten rows with real answers are worth more than a hundred names copied into a CRM. The test of the list is whether it changes what you do on Monday.
